summary: Glass Orbit is an interactive 3D space-weather mission trainer set inside a 360-degree glass observatory for young learners (ages 7–12). Powered by real NASA DONKI Coronal Mass Ejection (CME) telemetry and educational toolkits from NASA and the Canadian Space Agency (CSA), players face 5-turn solar-storm scenarios where they must balance Power, Life Support, Shields, and Scientific Evidence using tactile 3D mission cards. A 3-tier telemetry pipeline connects live to NASA's DONKI CME API with local caching and a SHA-256 verified offline snapshot so classrooms never lose access. After each mission, our adaptive NOVA coach analyzes decision latency and play style to deliver causal feedback, 3 actionable STEM tips, and one-click JSON/CSV report exports. Bilingual English/Traditional Chinese switching and a low-power Performance Mode ensure accessibility across devices.
details:
What It Does and How It Works

Glass Orbit turns real NASA space-weather data into a hands-on 3D orbital strategy game inside a 360-degree observatory. Players inspect a real NASA DONKI Coronal Mass Ejection (CME) alert, manage four mission pillars (Power, Life Support, Shields, and Scientific Evidence) over 5 turns, and play mission cards such as Solar Window, Storm Shield, Power Reserve, Life Support, Lunar Hydroponics, and CME Arrival Forecast while watching 3D resource pillars and particle effects respond in real time.

Benefits and Educational Impact

Designed for junior astronauts (ages 7–12) and STEM classrooms, the game replaces passive slides with real cause-and-effect trade-offs. Students learn why protecting a lunar or Martian outpost during a solar storm requires balancing survival with scientific observation. After each mission, our Adaptive NOVA Coach reviews the player's decision timing and resource choices, identifies their command style (Cautious Planner, Balanced Commander, or Bold Tactician), gives 3 practical STEM tips, and lets students or teachers export JSON and CSV mission logs.

Creativity and Design Considerations

1. High-Contrast 360-Degree Observatory: A crisp monochrome observatory console frames full-color 3D celestial bodies (Sun, Earth, Moon, Mars, and an asteroid belt) textured with NASA public-domain imagery so young learners stay focused on telemetry.

2. Three-Tier Telemetry Reliability: The app queries NASA's live DONKI CME API, falls back to browser-cached telemetry, and includes a SHA-256 verified offline snapshot (2024-05-10T07:12:00-CME-001) so school networks or offline demos never break.

3. Bilingual and Low-Power Friendly: An in-scene 3D dial switches the entire observatory between English and Traditional Chinese live, and a Performance Mode toggle reduces shadows, resolution scaling, and particles for older classroom laptops.

4. Honest Educational Framing: The interface clearly states that card points and turn rules are simplified educational models rather than flight-certified NASA specs, and no official NASA or CSA logos are used.

Tools, Coding Languages, and Software

Frontend and 3D: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Zustand.

Data and Hosting: NASA DONKI REST API, Node.js SHA-256 snapshot verification, GitHub Pages.

Demo Soundtrack: Synthesized directly as soft ambient mathematical waveforms (sub-bass, detuned ambient pad, soft bell arpeggio, and stereo delay) using Python's standard library (see audio/generate_space_bgm.py in the repository), with zero generative AI audio models or copyrighted samples.
